questions.question: Citizenship provisions are given in which part of the Indian Constitution?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Part II**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/e3594069eb4eac3d559af7c626aabe4ee4145967932cf8ad78e35476f134a4b8.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• **Part II** of the **Indian Constitution** comprises **Articles 5 to 11**, which govern the legal framework for **Citizenship** in India.
 
• These provisions specifically identified the persons who became citizens of India at the **commencement of the Constitution** on **January 26, 1950**, based on parameters like domicile, migration, and origin.
 
• **Article 11** is a significant provision that empowers the **Parliament of India** to make any law regarding the **acquisition and termination** of citizenship and all other related matters.
 
• Exercising this constitutional power, the **Parliament** enacted the **Citizenship Act of 1955**, which provides a comprehensive set of rules for citizenship after the initial constitutional phase.
 
• India adopts the principle of **Single Citizenship**, a concept borrowed from the **British Constitution**, which ensures that all citizens have the same rights across the entire nation, regardless of the state in which they reside.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/3e20068b61817b168623bbf4377a66602deb382bfb1e34ae29a5e35078dcefcb.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Part I** of the Constitution includes **Articles 1 to 4** and deals with **The Union and its Territory**, outlining the territorial jurisdiction and the power to form or alter states.
 
• **Part III** encompasses **Articles 12 to 35**, which enumerate the **Fundamental Rights**, the basic civil liberties guaranteed to individuals to protect them from the arbitrary exercise of state power.
 
• **Part IV** contains **Articles 36 to 51**, representing the **Directive Principles of State Policy (DPSP)**, which are non-justiciable guidelines for the state to establish social and economic democracy and a **Welfare State**.
 
• The **Citizenship Act, 1955** defines five ways to acquire citizenship: **Birth**, **Descent**, **Registration**, **Naturalization**, and **Incorporation of Territory**, while also providing for its loss through **Renunciation**, **Termination**, and **Deprivation**.

questions.question: Who has the power to create new states and alter boundaries of existing states?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Parliament**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/e3594069eb4eac3d559af7c626aabe4ee4145967932cf8ad78e35476f134a4b8.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• According to **Article 3** of the **Constitution of India**, the power to form new states and alter the areas, boundaries, or names of existing states is vested solely in the **Union Parliament**.
 
• This authority allows **Parliament** to increase the area of any state, diminish the area of any state, or change the name of any state through a simple legislative process that does not require a complex constitutional amendment.
 
• A bill for the reorganization of states can be introduced in either **House of Parliament** (the **Lok Sabha** or the **Rajya Sabha**) only after receiving the **prior recommendation of the President**.
 
• Before making such a recommendation, the **President** must refer the bill to the concerned **State Legislature** to express its views within a specified timeframe, although these views are **not binding** on the **Union Parliament**.
 
• The **Parliament** can proceed to pass the bill by a **simple majority** of the members present and voting, reflecting the **unitary bias** of the Indian federal system regarding territorial integrity.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/3e20068b61817b168623bbf4377a66602deb382bfb1e34ae29a5e35078dcefcb.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Article 2 and Article 4**

 
 
• **Article 2** empowers **Parliament** to admit or establish new states into the **Union of India** that were not previously part of its territory.
 
• **Article 4** clarifies that laws made under **Article 2** and **Article 3** are not to be considered amendments to the **Constitution** under **Article 368**, ensuring the process remains flexible.
 
 
 
• **Role of Other Entities**
 
 
• **President of India**: Acts as a facilitator by providing the mandatory prior recommendation for the bill but does not possess the legislative power to alter boundaries independently.
 
• **State Legislature**: Its role is strictly **consultative**; it cannot block the **Parliament** from redrawing boundaries even if it disagrees with the proposal.
 
• **Supreme Court**: While the **Judiciary** can exercise **judicial review** over the legality of the process, it has no power to create states or define territorial limits.
 
 
 
• **Indestructible Union**
 
 
• India is often described as an **indestructible Union of destructible states** because the **Parliament** can change the political map of the country at its discretion without the consent of the states.

questions.question: Which deity is predominantly worshipped through Manipuri dance?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Krishna**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/e3594069eb4eac3d559af7c626aabe4ee4145967932cf8ad78e35476f134a4b8.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• **Manipuri Dance**, also known as **Jagoi**, is one of the eight major **Indian classical dance** forms, originating from the northeastern state of **Manipur**.
 
• While the dance form has ancient roots in the pre-Hindu festival of **Lai Haraoba**, its classical identity is predominantly centered on **Vaishnavism**, which focuses on the devotion to **Lord Krishna**.
 
• The most significant theme in the Manipuri repertoire is the **Raslila**, a divine dance-drama that depicts the eternal love and spiritual connection between **Radha** and **Krishna**.
 
• The performance is characterized by its **Lasya** style, emphasizing gentle, fluid, and circular movements that reflect a meditative and devotional state (**Bhakti**) rather than dramatic or aggressive posturing.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/3e20068b61817b168623bbf4377a66602deb382bfb1e34ae29a5e35078dcefcb.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Historical Context**:

 
 
• The formalization of the **Vaishnavite** Manipuri dance is largely attributed to **King Bhagyachandra** (reigned 1763−1798), who codified the **Raslila** after having a spiritual vision of **Krishna**.
 
• He introduced the unique **Kumil** costume, a stiff, barrel-shaped skirt decorated with gold and silver embroidery and mirrors, designed to hide the dancer's leg movements and create a gliding effect.
 
 
 
• **Role of Shiva and Other Deities**:
 
 
• **Shiva** is worshipped in the ancient **Lai Haraoba** tradition as **Nongpok Ningthou**, alongside **Parvati** (Panthoibi), representing the older indigenous beliefs of the **Meitei** people.
 
• Despite these older roots, the **classical** form recognized today focuses almost exclusively on the life of **Krishna** as narrated in the **Bhagavata Purana** and the **Gita Govinda** by **Jayadeva**.
 
 
 
• **Rhythmic Elements**:
 
 
• The **Pung** (a traditional drum) is central to the dance; the **Pung Cholom** is a masculine performance where dancers play the drum while performing acrobatic jumps and turns.

questions.question: In which year did the Jaipur Literature Festival begin?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**2006**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/e3594069eb4eac3d559af7c626aabe4ee4145967932cf8ad78e35476f134a4b8.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• The **Jaipur Literature Festival (JLF)**, frequently described as the 'greatest literary show on Earth', held its very first edition in the year **2006**.
 
• It was co-founded by acclaimed writers **Namita Gokhale** and **William Dalrymple** with the vision of creating a democratic and inclusive platform for literary exchange.
 
• The inaugural event in **2006** was a modest gathering that featured approximately **18 writers**, including notable figures like **Hari Kunzru** and **Shobhaa De**, and attracted a small audience of a few hundred people.
 
• The festival is traditionally hosted at the historic **Diggi Palace Hotel** in the heart of **Jaipur**, the capital city of **Rajasthan**, providing a majestic backdrop for intellectual discourse.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/3e20068b61817b168623bbf4377a66602deb382bfb1e34ae29a5e35078dcefcb.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Organizational Structure**:

 
 
• The festival is produced by **Teamwork Arts**, led by Managing Director **Sanjoy K. Roy**, which oversees the massive logistics of the international event.
 
• It has grown into the world's largest **free literary festival**, though it now offers delegate packages for enhanced access.
 
 
 
• **Global Footprint**:
 
 
• Following its success in **India**, the festival has expanded globally with satellite editions in locations such as **London (British Library)**, **Boulder (Colorado)**, **Adelaide**, and **Doha**.
 
• It hosts a wide array of speakers, including **Nobel laureates**, **Booker Prize winners**, and **Sahitya Akademi** awardees, covering themes from **artificial intelligence** to **ancient history**.

questions.question: Which of the following plate boundaries formed the Himalayas?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Convergent boundary**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/e3594069eb4eac3d559af7c626aabe4ee4145967932cf8ad78e35476f134a4b8.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• The **Himalayas** were formed as a result of the collision between the **Indo-Australian Plate** and the **Eurasian Plate**.
 
• This tectonic interaction began approximately **40 to 50 million years ago** during the **Cenozoic Era**, leading to the closure of the **Tethys Ocean** that once existed between the two landmasses.
 
• A **convergent boundary** occurs where two tectonic plates move toward each other. In the case of the Himalayas, it is specifically a **continent-continent collision**.
 
• Because both continental plates have relatively low density, neither could be easily **subducted** into the mantle. This caused the crust to thicken and fold upward, creating the world's highest **mountain range**.
 
• The process is still ongoing today, as the **Indian Plate** continues to move northwards at a rate of about **5 cm per year**, causing the Himalayas to rise and making the region highly **seismically active**.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/3e20068b61817b168623bbf4377a66602deb382bfb1e34ae29a5e35078dcefcb.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Divergent Boundary**:

 
 
• Characterized by plates moving away from each other.
 
• Leads to the formation of **mid-oceanic ridges** and **rift valleys**, such as the **Great Rift Valley** in Africa.
 
 
 
• **Transform Boundary**:
 
 
• Involves plates sliding horizontally past one another.
 
• The **San Andreas Fault** is a prime example, where crust is neither created nor destroyed, but significant **earthquake activity** occurs.
 
 
 
• **Hotspot Boundary**:
 
 
• Technically not a boundary but a volcanic area located above a **mantle plume**.
 
• Responsible for the formation of island chains like **Hawaii** and geological features like the **Deccan Traps** in India.
 
 
 
• **Fold Mountains**:
 
 
• The Himalayas are classified as **young fold mountains**, distinguished by their rugged relief and high conical peaks.

questions.question: Why are the days on Venus longer than its years?

options.text: Venus has a slower rotation than revolution
Venus revolves very slowly around the Sun
Venus spins on its axis in the opposite direction

questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Venus has a slower rotation than revolution**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/e3594069eb4eac3d559af7c626aabe4ee4145967932cf8ad78e35476f134a4b8.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• Venus takes approximately **243 Earth days** to complete a single **rotation** on its axis, making it the slowest rotating planet in our **Solar System**.
 
• The planet completes one **revolution** or orbit around the **Sun** in about **225 Earth days**.
 
• Because the time taken to rotate (**sidereal day**) is longer than the time taken to orbit (**orbital period**), a day on Venus is technically longer than its year.
 
• This unusually slow rotation is theorized to be the result of **solar tidal torques** acting on the planet's thick atmosphere, which gradually decelerated its spin over **billions of years**.
 
• Venus is nearly a perfect sphere and has a very small **axial tilt** of about **3 degrees**, meaning it does not experience significant seasonal variations like Earth.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/3e20068b61817b168623bbf4377a66602deb382bfb1e34ae29a5e35078dcefcb.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Retrograde Rotation**:

 
 
• Venus exhibits **retrograde motion**, meaning it rotates in the **opposite direction** (clockwise) compared to most other planets (counter-clockwise).
 
• This results in the **Sun** rising in the **West** and setting in the **East**.
 
 
 
• **Solar Day vs. Sidereal Day**:
 
 
• While the **sidereal day** is 243 Earth days, the **solar day** (the time from one sunrise to the next) is only **117 Earth days** due to the combination of its retrograde spin and orbital path.
 
 
 
• **Atmospheric Pressure**:
 
 
• The surface of Venus is characterized by an **extreme greenhouse effect** and a surface pressure **92 times** that of Earth, roughly equivalent to the pressure 1,000 meters underwater.

questions.question: Which planet has a magnetic field that is offset from its center and tilted about 59 degrees to its rotational axis?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Uranus**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/e3594069eb4eac3d559af7c626aabe4ee4145967932cf8ad78e35476f134a4b8.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• **Uranus** possesses a highly unusual and irregular **magnetosphere**. Unlike most planets where the magnetic field is roughly aligned with the rotation, Uranus's magnetic axis is tilted at an extreme angle of **59 degrees** relative to its **rotational axis**.
 
• The magnetic field of **Uranus** is not generated from its geometric center; instead, it is **offset** by approximately **one-third of the planetary radius** (about 8,000 kilometers).
 
• This asymmetric magnetic field leads to a complex, twisting **magnetotail** that spirals behind the planet as it orbits the **Sun**.
 
• Data regarding these unique characteristics were primarily captured by the **Voyager 2** spacecraft during its historic flyby in **January 1986**.
 
• Scientists believe this offset field is produced by motion within a **conducting layer** of salty, pressurized fluid (an 'icy' mantle of water, methane, and ammonia) rather than in a deep metallic core.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/3e20068b61817b168623bbf4377a66602deb382bfb1e34ae29a5e35078dcefcb.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• The magnetic field configurations of other planets differ significantly:
 
 
• **Earth**: The magnetic field is roughly **dipolar** and tilted at a modest angle of approximately **11 degrees** from its rotational axis.
 
• **Jupiter**: It has the strongest magnetic field of any planet, tilted about **10 degrees** from its axis of rotation and slightly offset from the center.
 
• **Saturn**: It is unique for having a magnetic field almost perfectly aligned with its rotational axis, with a tilt of **less than 1 degree**.
 
• **Neptune**: Similar to Uranus, Neptune also has a highly tilted (**47 degrees**) and offset magnetic field, likely due to similar internal fluid dynamics.

questions.question: What is the maximum duration of a standard boxing bout in the Olympics?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Three 3-min rounds**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/e3594069eb4eac3d559af7c626aabe4ee4145967932cf8ad78e35476f134a4b8.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• Standard **Olympic boxing** matches for **men** consist of **three rounds**, with each round lasting exactly **three minutes**.
 
• A **one-minute rest interval** is provided between each round, allowing boxers to recover and receive instructions from their coaches.
 
• The bouts are scored using the **10-point must system**, where **five judges** evaluate the performance based on the number of quality blows landed, technical superiority, and competitiveness.
 
• The **International Olympic Committee (IOC)** oversees the regulations for these events, ensuring that the high-intensity nature of **amateur boxing** is maintained within this time frame.
 
• The match can end before the completion of the three rounds if the **referee** stops the contest (RSC), a boxer is **knocked out** (KO), or through disqualification.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/3e20068b61817b168623bbf4377a66602deb382bfb1e34ae29a5e35078dcefcb.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Women's Olympic Boxing**:

 
 
• Historically, women's bouts consisted of **four rounds** lasting **two minutes** each, though rules have seen adjustments to align more closely with male standards in various international competitions.
 
 
 
• **Equipment and Safety**:
 
 
• Since the **2016 Rio Olympics**, male boxers no longer wear **headguards**, whereas they remain mandatory for **female boxers**.
 
• Boxers use specific **gloves** weight (typically **10oz** or **12oz**) depending on the weight category to ensure safety.
 
 
 
• **Professional vs. Amateur**:
 
 
• While **Olympic (amateur) boxing** focuses on speed and technique over three rounds, **professional boxing** matches can last up to **12 rounds** for championship titles.

questions.question: How many Asian Games medals did India win in shooting at Hangzhou 2023?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**22**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/e3594069eb4eac3d559af7c626aabe4ee4145967932cf8ad78e35476f134a4b8.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• India achieved its most successful performance in the sport of **shooting** at the **19th Asian Games** held in **Hangzhou**, China, in 2023.
 
• The Indian shooting contingent secured a total of **22 medals**, comprising **7 gold**, **9 silver**, and **6 bronze** medals, marking a historic milestone for the country in this discipline.
 
• This performance shattered India's previous best shooting medal haul at the Asian Games, which was **14 medals** achieved during the **2006 Doha Games**.
 
• The **shooting** events contributed the highest number of gold medals to India's overall tally during the early phase of the competition, helping the nation cross the **100-medal threshold** for the first time.
 
• Individual brilliance was seen from shooters like **Sift Kaur Samra**, who won gold in the women's 50m rifle 3 positions, and **Palak Gulia**, who clinched gold in the women's 10m air pistol event.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/3e20068b61817b168623bbf4377a66602deb382bfb1e34ae29a5e35078dcefcb.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• The **19th Asian Games** were rescheduled from 2022 to **September 23 to October 8, 2023**, and featured 40 sports with athletes from 45 nations.
 
• **Shooting Highlights**:
 
 
• **World Records**: Indian shooters set multiple records, including a **world record** score of 1893.7 by the **Men's 10m Air Rifle Team** (Rudrankksh Patil, Aishwary Pratap Singh Tomar, and Divyansh Singh Panwar).
 
• **Sift Kaur Samra** created a new **World Record** in the individual 50m Rifle 3 Positions final with a score of 469.6.
 
• **Multi-medalists**: **Aishwary Pratap Singh Tomar** emerged as one of the most successful athletes, winning 4 medals in total across team and individual events.
 
 
 
• **Overall India Performance**:
 
 
• India finished in **fourth place** in the overall medal standings, behind China, Japan, and South Korea.
 
• The final medal count for India was **107** (28 gold, 38 silver, and 41 bronze), which is their highest-ever tally in the history of the **Asian Games**.

questions.question: Blood is classified under which type of animal tissue?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Connective tissue**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/e3594069eb4eac3d559af7c626aabe4ee4145967932cf8ad78e35476f134a4b8.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• **Blood** is a specialized type of **fluid connective tissue** that plays a vital role in maintaining the body internal environment by circulating through the cardiovascular system.
 
• Biologically, it is classified as a connective tissue because it originates from the **embryonic mesoderm**, just like other connective tissues such as bone and cartilage.
 
• It consists of a straw-colored liquid extracellular matrix known as **plasma**, which constitutes nearly **55%** of the total blood volume, and **formed elements** making up the remaining **45%**.
 
• The **formed elements** are comprised of three main types of cells: **Erythrocytes** (Red Blood Cells) for oxygen transport, **Leukocytes** (White Blood Cells) for immune defense, and **Thrombocytes** (Platelets) for blood clotting.
 
• A unique characteristic of blood compared to other connective tissues is that its matrix is **fluid** and it lacks structural **fibers** like collagen or elastin under normal physiological conditions; however, **fibrin fibers** are formed during the process of **coagulation**.
 
• The primary functions of blood include the transport of **metabolic wastes** to the kidneys, delivery of **hormones** to target organs, and the regulation of **body temperature** and **pH levels**.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/3e20068b61817b168623bbf4377a66602deb382bfb1e34ae29a5e35078dcefcb.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Epithelial tissue**:

 
 
• Forms the **outer covering** of the body and the **lining** of internal organs and cavities.
 
• Cells are tightly packed with minimal **intercellular space** and rest on a **basement membrane**.
 
 
 
• **Muscular tissue**:
 
 
• Comprised of elongated cells called **muscle fibers** that contain contractile proteins like **actin** and **myosin**.
 
• It is divided into three types: **skeletal** (voluntary), **smooth** (involuntary), and **cardiac** (heart muscle).
 
 
 
• **Nervous tissue**:
 
 
• Specialized for the **conduction of electrical impulses** throughout the body to coordinate functions.
 
• Main components include **neurons** (nerve cells) and **neuroglial cells** which provide support and insulation.

questions.question: Which of the following is an example of chemotropism in plants?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Pollen tube growing towards ovule**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/e3594069eb4eac3d559af7c626aabe4ee4145967932cf8ad78e35476f134a4b8.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• **Chemotropism** is a biological phenomenon where the growth or movement of a plant part occurs in response to a **chemical stimulus**.
 
• In flowering plants, the growth of the **pollen tube** towards the **ovule** is a classic example of **positive chemotropism**.
 
• When a **pollen grain** lands on the **stigma**, it germinates to form a tube that travels through the **style**.
 
• The **ovule** secretes certain **chemical substances** (such as sugars or specific proteins) that act as attractants, guiding the **pollen tube** directly to the **embryo sac** for fertilization.
 
• This directional growth ensures that the **male gametes** reach the **female gamete** (egg cell) efficiently within the **ovary**.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/3e20068b61817b168623bbf4377a66602deb382bfb1e34ae29a5e35078dcefcb.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Phototropism**:

 
 
• It involves the bending of plant **shoots** towards a **light source**.
 
• The hormone **Auxin** facilitates this by promoting cell elongation on the shaded side of the stem.
 
 
 
• **Geotropism** (Gravitropism):
 
 
• This is the growth of plant parts in response to **gravity**.
 
• **Roots** typically exhibit **positive geotropism** by growing downwards into the soil, while shoots show negative geotropism.
 
 
 
• **Thigmonasty**:
 
 
• This is a **non-directional** movement triggered by **touch**, famously seen in the **Mimosa pudica** (Touch-me-not) plant.
 
• Unlike tropisms, which are growth-related, this movement is caused by rapid **turgor pressure** changes in specialized cells called the **pulvinus**.

questions.question: The Chipko Movement is associated with:
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Forest conservation**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/e3594069eb4eac3d559af7c626aabe4ee4145967932cf8ad78e35476f134a4b8.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• The **Chipko Movement** was a transformative environmental uprising that began in the **early 1970s** in the **Garhwal Himalayas** of **Uttarakhand** (formerly part of Uttar Pradesh) to protest against large-scale **deforestation**.
 
• The movement is famously named after the Hindi word **Chipko**, which means **to hug** or **to cling**, as the protesters would physically embrace trees to prevent loggers from cutting them down.
 
• It was primarily a **non-violent** struggle led by rural villagers, particularly **women**, who depended on the forests for their basic needs like fodder, fuel, and water.
 
• The first major protest occurred in **1973** in **Mandal village** of the **Alaknanda Valley**, eventually spreading throughout the Himalayan region and influencing environmental policies across **India**.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/3e20068b61817b168623bbf4377a66602deb382bfb1e34ae29a5e35078dcefcb.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Key Figures of the Movement**:

 
 
• **Sunderlal Bahuguna**: An eminent environmentalist who gave the movement a proper direction and coined the famous slogan **Ecology is permanent economy**. He undertook a **5,000-kilometer trans-Himalaya march** to spread awareness.
 
• **Gaura Devi**: A courageous peasant woman who led the mobilization of women in **Reni village** in **1974**, successfully forcing the contractors to retreat.
 
• **Chandi Prasad Bhatt**: A social activist and pioneer of the movement who founded the **Dasholi Gram Swarajya Sangh (DGSS)**, which became a breeding ground for the struggle.
 
 
 
• **Impact**:
 
 
• The movement led to a significant victory in **1980** when Prime Minister **Indira Gandhi** enacted a **15-year ban** on commercial tree felling in the Himalayan forests of **Uttar Pradesh**.
 
• It inspired several other movements, most notably the **Appiko Movement** in **Karnataka** (1983), which focused on protecting the **Western Ghats**.

questions.question: The Rs. 6000 crores allocated for One Nation One Subscription initiative ensures smooth implementation of ONOS from 1st January 2025 to 31st December _______.
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**2027**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/e3594069eb4eac3d559af7c626aabe4ee4145967932cf8ad78e35476f134a4b8.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• The **Union Cabinet**, chaired by **Prime Minister Narendra Modi**, approved the **One Nation One Subscription (ONOS)** scheme in **November 2024** to provide unified access to scientific journals.
 
• The scheme is a **Central Sector Scheme** designed to benefit students, faculty, and researchers across all government-funded **Higher Educational Institutions** and **Research and Development** laboratories.
 
• The government has allocated a total financial outlay of **Rs. 6,069 crore** to support the implementation of this massive digital resource initiative.
 
• The approved duration for this phase of the **One Nation One Subscription** initiative spans **three calendar years**, beginning on **1st January 2025** and concluding on **31st December 2027**.
 
• This initiative aims to eliminate the disparity in access to **scientific knowledge** between premier institutions like **IITs** and smaller regional universities by providing a **national-level subscription**.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/3e20068b61817b168623bbf4377a66602deb382bfb1e34ae29a5e35078dcefcb.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Operational Framework**:

 
 
• The **Ministry of Education** will serve as the nodal ministry, with the **Information and Library Network (INFLIBNET) Centre** acting as the primary executing agency.
 
• The **Anusandhan National Research Foundation (ANRF)** will also play a role in periodic reviews and impact assessment of the scheme.
 
 
 
• **Scope and Reach**:
 
 
• The program will provide access to nearly **13,000 international journals** and a vast array of **conference proceedings** and **databases** from global publishers.
 
• It is expected to benefit over **1.8 crore students** and researchers, significantly boosting India’s **Global Innovation Index** ranking.
 
• The **One Nation One Subscription** model is a key pillar of the **National Education Policy (NEP) 2020**, focusing on the democratization of research tools.

questions.concept: India under East India Company’s Rule
questions.question: Which crop did the British force the peasants of Maharashtra to produce?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Cotton**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/e3594069eb4eac3d559af7c626aabe4ee4145967932cf8ad78e35476f134a4b8.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• The British colonial administration followed a policy of **commercialization of agriculture** in India to transform the country into a supplier of raw materials for British industries.
 
• The **Deccan Plateau**, encompassing large parts of **Maharashtra**, was specifically targeted for **Cotton** production because of its fertile **Black Soil** (also known as **Regur Soil**), which is ideal for moisture retention and cotton growth.
 
• The **Industrial Revolution** in Britain, particularly the growth of the textile industry in **Manchester** and **Lancashire**, created a massive demand for cheap, high-quality raw cotton.
 
• The **American Civil War** (1861−1865) disrupted cotton supplies from the United States to Britain, leading the British to forcefully expand cotton cultivation in the **Bombay Presidency** and **Maharashtra** to fill the supply gap.
 
• Peasants were coerced into growing these **cash crops** instead of food grains through the imposition of high **land revenue** under the **Ryotwari System**, forcing them to borrow from **moneylenders** and enter a cycle of chronic indebtedness.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/3e20068b61817b168623bbf4377a66602deb382bfb1e34ae29a5e35078dcefcb.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• The British forced different regions to specialize in specific crops:
 
 
• **Tea**: Cultivation was heavily promoted in **Assam** and the hills of **Darjeeling** through the plantation system.
 
• **Jute**: Peasants in **Bengal** were forced to produce jute to meet the global demand for gunny bags and packaging materials.
 
• **Indigo**: Primarily cultivated in **Bengal** and **Bihar**, which eventually led to the **Indigo Revolt** of 1859.
 
• **Sugarcane**: The **United Provinces** (present-day Uttar Pradesh) was the primary center for sugarcane production.
 
• **Wheat**: Cultivation was encouraged in **Punjab** to ensure food security for the British army and for export to Europe.
 
 
 
• The forced cultivation of cash crops over food crops often resulted in severe **famines** and agrarian unrest, such as the **Deccan Riots** of 1875 in **Maharashtra**.

questions.concept: Socio - Religious Reform Movements in the 19th and 20th CE India
questions.question: In which year the World Parliament of Religions was held in Chicago?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**1893**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/e3594069eb4eac3d559af7c626aabe4ee4145967932cf8ad78e35476f134a4b8.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• The first **World’s Parliament of Religions** was held from **September 11 to September 27, 1893**, in **Chicago**, Illinois, United States.
 
• It was organized as part of the **World’s Columbian Exposition**, an international fair commemorating the **400th anniversary** of **Christopher Columbus’s** arrival in the New World in **1492**.
 
• This event was a landmark moment in global history, representing the first formal attempt to create a global dialogue between the faiths of the **East** and the **West**, including **Hinduism**, **Buddhism**, **Jainism**, and **Islam**.
 
• **Swami Vivekananda**, representing **Hinduism** and **India**, delivered a historic speech on the opening day, **September 11, 1893**, which began with the iconic greeting, 'Sisters and brothers of America!'.
 
• The parliament aimed to find common ground between different religions and promote **universal tolerance**, which significantly influenced the modern **Interfaith movement**.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/3e20068b61817b168623bbf4377a66602deb382bfb1e34ae29a5e35078dcefcb.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Foundational Context and Organizers:**

 
 
• The parliament was the brainchild of **Charles Carroll Bonney**, a prominent lawyer and **Swedenborgian** layman, who served as the president of the **World’s Congress Auxiliary**.
 
• The meetings were held at the **Permanent Memorial Art Palace**, which today serves as the world-renowned **Art Institute of Chicago**.
 
• Apart from Vivekananda, other significant participants included **Virchand Gandhi**, who represented **Jainism**, and **Anagarika Dharmapala**, who represented **Theravada Buddhism**.
 
• The event played a pivotal role in introducing **Eastern philosophies**, particularly **Yoga** and **Vedanta**, to the Western audience, sparking widespread interest in **Indian spirituality**.
 
• In **2012**, the site of the speech was renamed **Swami Vivekananda Way** to honor his contribution to religious harmony and his role in the 1893 assembly.

questions.question: Which of the following ministry has unveiled 'Logistics Ease Across Different States (LEADS) 2024' Report?

options.text: Ministry of Ports, Shipping and Waterways

questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Ministry of Commerce & Industry**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/e3594069eb4eac3d559af7c626aabe4ee4145967932cf8ad78e35476f134a4b8.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• The **Logistics Ease Across Different States (LEADS) 2024** report was released by the **Union Ministry of Commerce & Industry** to evaluate the efficiency of the logistics ecosystem across India.
 
• The report is prepared by the **Department for Promotion of Industry and Internal Trade (DPIIT)**, providing a comprehensive assessment based on both perception and objective data from stakeholders.
 
• The primary objective of **LEADS** is to foster **competitive federalism**, encouraging states and Union Territories to improve their infrastructure and regulatory frameworks to reduce overall **logistics costs**.
 
• The **2024 edition** marks the **sixth version** of this indigenous index, which was first introduced in **2018** to track progress in the logistics sector.
 
• This initiative is a critical component of the **National Logistics Policy (NLP)** and the **PM GatiShakti National Master Plan**, aiming to streamline multi-modal transport and supply chain management.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/3e20068b61817b168623bbf4377a66602deb382bfb1e34ae29a5e35078dcefcb.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• Performance Categorization:
 
 
• **Achievers**: States and Union Territories that demonstrate exceptional performance and efficient logistics ecosystems.
 
• **Fast Movers**: States that have initiated significant reforms and are showing rapid improvement in their logistics indicators.
 
• **Aspirers**: Regions that are in the early stages of developing modern logistics infrastructure and streamlining processes.
 
 
 
• Three Core Pillars of Assessment:
 
 
• **Logistics Infrastructure**: Evaluates the quality and availability of **road networks**, **rail connectivity**, **warehousing**, and **air cargo** facilities.
 
• **Logistics Services**: Focuses on the efficiency and reliability of transport providers, terminal operators, and value-added services.
 
• **Operating and Regulatory Environment**: Assesses the ease of obtaining permits, the impact of government facilitation, and the degree of digitalization in logistics processes.
 
 
 
• The **LEADS** report acts as a feedback mechanism for the government to identify bottlenecks and implement targeted interventions, such as the **Unified Logistics Interface Platform (ULIP)**, to enhance trade competitiveness.
